energyContext.title: Electricity costs are changing. Your energy plan should, too.
energyContext.subtitle: Texas residential electricity prices have risen over the past several years while the grid prepares for substantial new demand. Solar can reduce a property's exposure to purchased electricity, but actual results depend on usage, utility rules, system design, financing, and how much solar energy is consumed on-site.
energyContext.card1Details: 2021: 12.11¢/kWh → 2024: 14.94¢/kWh. Statewide average across all Texas residential customers. Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-861.
energyContext.card2Details: January–May 2026 Texas residential average: 16.15¢/kWh vs. 15.14¢/kWh for the same period in 2025. These are preliminary year-to-date figures, not finalized annual values. Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Electric Power Monthly.
energyContext.card3Label: Data centers drive projected load growth
energyContext.card3Details: ERCOT’s 2025 long-term load forecast identifies data centers as the largest category of projected new large-load growth. Actual build-out, timing and grid impact depend on interconnection, permitting, market conditions and policy decisions. This does not represent currently operational facilities alone.
energyContext.disclaimer: Data for informational purposes. Verify all claims against primary sources before making decisions. Solar results vary by property, utility and system design.
calc.dentonNote: Denton: exported energy credited at $0.05/kWh, not retail rate.
calc.dentonDisclaimer: Estimated planning result. A bill-based analysis is required for a precise Denton calculation.
calc.dentonSelfConsumptionHint: This is a planning assumption, not a measured value. Actual self-consumption depends on the home’s hourly energy use, solar production, system size, and battery operation.
calc.scenarioDisclaimer: Rate-change scenarios are assumptions for comparison only, not forecasts of future prices.
energyCosts.heroTitle: Texas electricity prices and what they mean for solar.
energyCosts.heroSubtitle: A focused review of verified electricity-price data, ERCOT demand projections, Denton-specific solar rules and what solar can and cannot guarantee.
energyCosts.section1Title: Texas residential electricity prices have risen steadily.
energyCosts.section1Body: From 2021 through 2024, the statewide average residential electricity price in Texas increased from 12.11¢/kWh to 14.94¢/kWh, a cumulative change of approximately 23.4%. This reflects annual averages reported by the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
energyCosts.section2Title: Not all published data represents a finalized annual value.
energyCosts.section2Body: The EIA publishes monthly data that becomes final only after the full calendar year is complete. Year-to-date figures (such as January–May 2025 or January–May 2026) are preliminary and should not be compared directly against finalized annual values without noting the distinction.
energyCosts.section3Title: The grid is preparing for substantial new demand.
energyCosts.section3Body: ERCOT’s 2025 long-term load forecast identifies data centers as the largest category of projected new large-load growth in its planning area. This forecast reflects requested and attested interconnection applications, not currently operational facilities alone.
energyCosts.section4Title: Projected load is not the same as guaranteed future consumption.
energyCosts.section4Body: ERCOT applies adjustment factors to TSP-provided load forecasts based on historical experience. Not all requested load will be built on the originally proposed timeline, and actual consumption may differ from requested interconnection capacity. These forecasts inform grid planning but do not independently determine residential electricity prices.
energyCosts.section5Title: Denton Municipal Electric operates under its own rate structure.
energyCosts.section5Body: Denton Municipal Electric (DME) is a municipally owned utility and is not subject to PUCT deregulated market rules. Since January 1, 2025, DME credits exported solar energy at $0.05/kWh — significantly less than the retail rate. This means exported solar energy does not offset grid purchases at a one-to-one rate.
energyCosts.section6Title: Solar can reduce the amount of electricity you purchase from the grid.
energyCosts.section6Body: A properly sized solar system can reduce a property’s exposure to purchased electricity by generating power on-site. The degree of reduction depends on system size, roof orientation, shade, energy consumption patterns, utility rules, and how much solar energy is consumed directly versus exported.
energyCosts.section7Title: Solar is a strong planning tool, not a guarantee against all future price changes.
energyCosts.section7Body: Solar does not eliminate fixed utility charges, does not guarantee a specific rate of return, and does not protect against all possible regulatory changes. Actual savings depend on usage, system design, financing, utility rules and evolving energy markets. A site-specific analysis is required before any proposal.

index.faq.q1: How does a home solar system work?
index.faq.a1: Solar panels convert sunlight into direct-current electricity. An inverter converts that power into alternating current your home can use. Depending on your design, excess production may flow to the utility grid or charge a battery.
index.faq.q2: How long can solar panels last?
index.faq.a2: Many modern panels are designed to operate for 25 years or more, although output gradually declines and warranties vary by manufacturer. Inverters and other components may have different replacement cycles.
index.faq.a3: No. Grid-tied solar can operate without storage. Batteries can add backup capability, time-of-use flexibility and more control, but the right choice depends on budget, outage concerns and utility rules.
index.faq.q4: Do panels work on cloudy or rainy days?
index.faq.a4: Yes, though production is usually lower than under direct sun. Annual energy modeling accounts for local weather patterns rather than assuming every day is perfectly clear.
index.faq.q5: How can solar affect property value?
index.faq.a5: Owned solar may contribute to buyer interest and perceived operating savings, but market impact varies. Financing structure, system condition, documentation and local appraisal practices all matter.
index.faq.q6: What size system should I get?
index.faq.a6: The right size depends on annual usage, roof area, orientation, shade, panel output, future loads such as EV charging, utility limits and your financial goals. Bigger is not automatically better.
